items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: Illinois Jacquet has a band that’s a very good band, and of course he’s from the old school

ctx.x: No, not necessarily doing the Basie thing, but in other words, just putting your thumb on the pulse and saying, are the traditions alive and well?

Yeah, I would say the traditions are alive and well. Illinois Jacquet has a band that’s a very good band, and of course he’s from the old school, and the arrangements are from that same school. And a lot of the guys are in that generation, mixed with younger guys, really doing very well. And there are some bands around New York, well I don’t know how you rate Toshiko Akiyoshi, but as far as I’m concerned she’s an excellent writer and she gets a lot of great sounds, chords and textures out of that band. Then the…
How often does that band play though?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: even Illinois Jacquet, who was with the Basie band for a minute... There’s another band out there led by Illinois Jacquet that some critics thought sounded more like the Basie band than the Basie band.

ctx.x: We can add him if you’d like. And Marshall Royal himself. All excellent soloists but most critics say that the greatest soloists were with the Old Testament band, the Lester Youngs, the Buck Claytons, Harry Edison, Earle Warren, Jack Washington on baritone and saxophone, Buddy Tate, Don Byas, even Illinois Jacquet, who was with the Basie band for a minute. Most critics seemed to favor the old soloists, the Old Testament band.
What do you think about that judgment?
